name: Light Cinnamon-Drab
lede: Light Cinnamon-Drab is a muted tan from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, filed again by name in the 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary, and one of the most common named colors in our painting archive.

sections.title: A Ridgway tone, common in paint
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature* carries this swatch on plate XLVI, hue 13″″″″, tone b [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary files the exact name "Light Cinnamon-Drab" under block 45, "light grayish reddish brown" [2]. The name builds "light" onto [[cinnamon-drab]], itself a compound of the spice word cinnamon and the muted drab family [1].

In our color library its closest neighbor is [[dusty-cinnamon]], about 3.0 units away, nearly the same color on screen, followed by [[mushroom]] at 3.2 units [3]. [[greyish-tan]] sits 3.6 units off and lighter, and [[light-brownish-drab]] 4.5 units off and redder [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive of 23,781 paintings matches this tone in 1,070 of them, about 4.5 percent, as photographed, more common than 86 percent of the named colors we track [4]. It peaks in the 1200s, present in 10 of the 142 paintings we have from that century, 1.8 times the rate its museums' own baseline would predict [4].

Inside a painting it most often plays a hidden color, in 44 percent of its 684 clearly-ranked appearances [4]. Constantin Hansen favors it most, in 8 of his 34 works here, 4.2 times his museums' baseline rate, and the tone is most over-represented in Nepal, 4.5 times the expected rate [4]. It shares canvases with Pale Greyish Vinaceous and Dark Vinaceous-Drab far more than chance, lifts of 8.4 and 7.0 [4]. The earliest dated match is the year 1000, 912 years before the name's first 1912 record, so this is a look-alike hue in an old photograph, not proof of the name's age [4]. The archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor, not a first.
